clinicalPearls: An X-linked disorder in males often described as Angelman-like, with severe intellectual disability, absent speech and a happy demeanour
Features include postnatal microcephaly, ataxia, epilepsy and a characteristic ocular finding of abnormal eye movements
Eye-movement abnormalities such as ophthalmoplegia and difficulty with voluntary gaze, along with truncal ataxia, are useful pointers
There is often progressive neurological decline over childhood, with loss of skills and cerebellar atrophy on imaging, unlike the static course of Angelman syndrome
Marked feeding difficulty, drooling and gastrointestinal problems are common
Caused by loss-of-function variants in SLC9A6, encoding the endosomal sodium-hydrogen exchanger NHE6; carrier females may show milder features
The combination of an Angelman-like phenotype with regression and eye-movement disorder suggests SLC9A6 rather than a classic Angelman cause
reference.pathophysiology: SLC9A6 encodes NHE6, a sodium-hydrogen exchanger located in the membranes of early and recycling endosomes, where it regulates intracellular (endosomal) pH and thereby the trafficking and signalling of receptors important for neuronal development and maintenance. Loss-of-function variants disturb endosomal acidification, impairing processes such as neurotrophin (TrkB) signalling and leading to accumulation of abnormal material and neuronal dysfunction. The result is a neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative picture with intellectual disability, epilepsy, ataxia, eye-movement disorder and progressive cerebellar atrophy. Because the gene is X-linked, males are affected while carrier females show variable, usually milder features.
additionalDifferentials: Other X-linked intellectual disability with ataxia
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI to detect cerebellar atrophy, sometimes progressive
Methylation and UBE3A studies to exclude Angelman syndrome
Targeted SLC9A6 sequencing or an X-linked intellectual-disability gene panel or exome sequencing
redFlags: Progressive loss of previously acquired skills
Feeding failure with aspiration and faltering growth
reference.prognosis: Christianson syndrome causes severe intellectual disability with a progressive neurodegenerative course, including cerebellar atrophy and worsening movement and feeding problems over time. Prognosis is guarded, and management is supportive and multidisciplinary.
pitfalls: Diagnosing Angelman syndrome clinically and stopping the workup when methylation testing is normal
Overlooking the progressive, neurodegenerative nature and cerebellar atrophy
Assuming carrier females are always unaffected
management: Control epilepsy with appropriate antiseizure medication tailored to the seizure types

Support feeding and nutrition with speech-and-language feeding assessment, management of drooling with antimuscarinic measures, gastrostomy where oral intake is unsafe, and treatment of reflux and constipation
Provide developmental therapies — physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech-and-language input with augmentative communication aids for the absent speech
Manage ataxia and movement difficulty with mobility aids and physiotherapy, monitoring for progressive neurological decline and cerebellar atrophy
Arrange ophthalmological assessment and support for the eye-movement disorder
Offer genetic counselling with carrier testing of female relatives, explaining X-linked inheritance and variable carrier features
Coordinate lifelong care through a paediatric neurology and neurodisability multidisciplinary team
